scenarios.title: €1,800 general services
scenarios.q: Which route is the normal starting point?
scenarios.feedback: The amount is within the low-value direct-award limit for goods/general services/works. Always assess the full foreseeable need rather than splitting it.

scenarios.title: €5,500 intellectual service
scenarios.q: Which route is the normal starting point?
scenarios.feedback: Intellectual services remain within the low-value direct-award limit up to €6,000. The full foreseeable need must still be assessed.

scenarios.title: €72,000 consultancy · extrabudgetary funding
scenarios.q: Which procurement route should you expect?
opts: Competitive Bidding + applicable Legal Compliance Review
scenarios.feedback: The value is above the low-value limit and below the international threshold. In the applicable extrabudgetary/mixed-funding band, the additional legal-compliance control forms part of the route.

scenarios.title: Three related purchases of €1,900 each
scenarios.q: Can the need be treated as three separate low-value procurements?
opts: No, assess the full foreseeable procurement need
Yes, if different staff request them
scenarios.feedback: Thresholds are based on the full foreseeable procurement need, not invoice-by-invoice or requester-by-requester.

scenarios.title: €190,000 foreseeable need
scenarios.q: Which procedure should be planned?
scenarios.feedback: At or above the €184,000 threshold, the international public-call route applies.

scenarios.title: Bid missing a non-essential item
scenarios.q: What is the safest next step when the missing information is genuinely non-essential?
opts: Use clarification without changing the offer
Let the bidder submit a new price
scenarios.feedback: Clarification can address non-essential missing information, but it must not alter the substance of the submitted offer.

scenarios.title: JP · one Budget Heading changes by +12%
scenarios.q: What is the formal route after the forecast review?
scenarios.feedback: For a Joint Programme, a relevant Budget Heading/subtotal variation within ±25% follows the Notification route.

scenarios.title: JP · one Budget Heading moves by +28%
scenarios.q: What formal route follows the forecast review?
scenarios.feedback: For a Joint Programme, assess the relevant Budget Heading/subtotal. A movement beyond ±25% follows the Addendum route.

scenarios.title: JP · all relevant Budget Headings remain within ±25%
scenarios.q: What is the formal route?
scenarios.feedback: The forecast is still prepared; the formal route is Notification when all relevant subtotal variations remain within the threshold.

scenarios.title: Forecast includes an extension of the project
scenarios.q: Which route governs?
scenarios.feedback: An extension is a contractual change and follows the Addendum route.

scenarios.title: Forecast changes total project cost
scenarios.q: Which route governs?
scenarios.feedback: A change in total cost requires the Addendum route.

scenarios.title: Multiple changes: +10% reallocation plus project extension
scenarios.q: How should the package be handled?
opts: One consolidated exercise; Addendum route governs
scenarios.feedback: Use one consolidated revised-budget exercise. If any selected change directly requires an Addendum, the Addendum route governs the package.

scenarios.title: Grant procedure · total budget €12,000
scenarios.q: What is the normal starting route?
scenarios.feedback: Below €15,000, the grant procedure starts with the Direct Award route.

scenarios.title: Grant procedure · total budget €18,000
scenarios.q: Which route should be used as the starting point?
scenarios.feedback: The threshold is assessed on the total procedure budget. At €18,000 the Competitive Call route is the normal starting point unless a permitted exception applies.

scenarios.title: Grant threshold question
scenarios.q: Which amount determines the route?
scenarios.feedback: The relevant threshold is the total budget of the grant procedure, not the amount awarded to each individual grantee.

scenarios.title: €22,000 grant with a permitted exception
scenarios.q: Which route can apply when the exception is properly supported?
scenarios.feedback: At or above €15,000, a permitted and properly justified exception can lead to the Exceptional Direct Award route.

scenarios.title: Evaluation begins before eligibility is checked
scenarios.q: What should be corrected?
opts: Apply the gates in sequence before award scoring
scenarios.feedback: Evaluation should preserve the required sequence and traceability: admissibility/exclusion/eligibility controls before the award assessment as applicable.

scenarios.title: Grant activity already completed before signature
scenarios.q: What is the core concern?
scenarios.feedback: The financed action should not already be completed; implementation timing must match the permitted period set in the grant arrangement.

scenarios.title: Service delivered in December · invoice arrives in January
scenarios.q: Which year-end issue should be assessed?
scenarios.feedback: The key question is when the service was delivered/rendered, not when cash is paid. The delivered portion belongs to the correct financial year and may require an accrual.

scenarios.title: Goods delivered in January
scenarios.q: Should this be recorded as prior-year expenditure?
opts: Yes, if the PO was created earlier
No, delivery is in the new year
Yes, if supplier invoiced in December
scenarios.feedback: The financial year follows delivery/performance. A January delivery is not prior-year expenditure.

scenarios.title: 2026 delivery and invoice available
scenarios.q: When can the PO be finalised?
opts: Once expenditure is recorded and the billed/invoice status is checked
scenarios.feedback: Finalisation is linked to the expenditure being recorded in FIMS/Fiche PO and the billing/invoice status being checked; it does not require waiting for cash payment.

scenarios.title: Cross-year service · invoice covers both years
scenarios.q: What is the correct approach?
opts: Charge the full invoice to the earlier year
Split according to the service/delivery periods
scenarios.feedback: Allocate the expenditure according to when the service was rendered. The later-year share follows the applicable prepaid/CCA treatment where relevant.

scenarios.title: Cross-year service · no invoice at closing
scenarios.q: What should be accrued?
opts: Only the portion delivered/rendered in the closing year
scenarios.feedback: Only the part delivered/rendered in the closing year is accrued. The later-year portion is not a prior-year provision.

scenarios.title: Annual-budget PO for next-year delivery
scenarios.q: What is the operational direction?
opts: Close/finalise the prior-year PO as appropriate and arrange the new-year PO
scenarios.feedback: For annual-budget treatment, next-year delivery requires the appropriate new-year PO/treatment rather than being charged to the closing year.

scenarios.title: Invoice received but no delivery/acceptance evidence
scenarios.q: Is the payment file ready?
scenarios.feedback: A payment file needs evidence that the goods/services/deliverables were received and accepted, not only the invoice.

scenarios.title: PO request has no contractual/procurement basis
scenarios.q: What should happen before the PO is created?
scenarios.feedback: The PO must be supported by the applicable procurement and contractual basis before financial commitment is completed.

scenarios.title: Payment follows an approved PO
scenarios.q: Does the approval route restart from zero?
opts: No, payment continues from the established contractual/PO basis and adds payment controls
scenarios.feedback: Payment should remain linked to the approved contractual and PO trail; it adds delivery, invoice and payment checks rather than rebuilding the whole case.

scenarios.title: Invoice amount differs from contract / PO
scenarios.q: What is the first control?
opts: Reconcile the invoice against the contractual and PO basis
scenarios.feedback: Resolve mismatches before payment. The invoice, accepted delivery and contractual/PO basis should align or be formally explained and corrected.

scenarios.title: Supplier bank details changed just before payment
scenarios.q: What is the safer approach?
opts: Verify the change through the controlled supplier/bank-data process before payment
scenarios.feedback: A late bank-detail change is a payment-risk flag and should be independently verified through the controlled process before funds are released.

scenarios.title: Work starts before contract signature
scenarios.q: What is the control issue?
opts: The contract should be in place before work starts, with the budgetary commitment/PO arranged as required
scenarios.feedback: The operational sequence should establish the contract and required budgetary commitment before execution starts.

scenarios.title: Starting a financial report
scenarios.q: What is the best first focus?
scenarios.feedback: A financial report starts from the current financial position: gather the data, reconcile and structure the report before finalising.

scenarios.title: Report figures do not reconcile
scenarios.q: What should happen before finalisation?
scenarios.feedback: A report should be reconciled before it is structured and finalised. Unexplained differences weaken reliability and the audit trail.

scenarios.title: Future expenditure needs to be revised
scenarios.q: Which companion process is relevant?
scenarios.feedback: Reporting explains where the project is now; forecast/budget revision addresses where expenditure is going and what needs to change.

scenarios.title: A correction changes forecast figures after review
scenarios.q: What should happen?
opts: Keep the old route decision automatically
Correct the figures and reassess the formal route if the change affects it
scenarios.feedback: When comments change figures, return to the working file, correct it and reassess the Notification/Addendum route if thresholds or contractual changes are affected.

scenarios.title: Working forecast file is still with Project Team
scenarios.q: Should the working file already be sent to DPC HQ?
opts: No, wait until the working cycle is completed and the clean package is prepared
scenarios.feedback: Keep the working file within the internal review cycle until it returns and the clean version is prepared for the applicable final route.

scenarios.title: VC at AP level
scenarios.q: Is donor acceptance automatically required for the budget revision?
opts: No, AP-level VC does not automatically require donor acceptance
scenarios.feedback: For AP-level VC, donor acceptance is not automatically required. Specific earmarked arrangements can have a different contractual requirement.

scenarios.title: Mission has not yet been authorised
scenarios.q: Should travel be treated as ready to proceed?
opts: Yes, expense claim can fix it later
No, complete the Mission Order / authorisation route first
scenarios.feedback: The mission workflow starts with authorisation. The later Expense Claim reimburses actual eligible expenses; it does not replace prior authorisation.

scenarios.title: Mission is completed
scenarios.q: What is the next connected workflow?
opts: Prepare the Expense Claim with supporting evidence
scenarios.feedback: After the mission takes place, the process moves to the Expense Claim and reimbursement evidence.

scenarios.title: Expense claim lacks travel evidence
scenarios.q: Is the file complete?
opts: No, add the supporting travel/expense evidence
scenarios.feedback: The claim should be supported by the relevant travel and expense evidence so the reimbursement trail is complete.

scenarios.title: Mission details change after authorisation
scenarios.q: What is the safest approach?
opts: Document and obtain the required update/approval before relying on the changed arrangement
scenarios.feedback: Material changes should remain traceable and follow the applicable update/approval route rather than appearing for the first time at reimbursement stage.

scenarios.title: Expense is claimed with no link to the authorised mission
scenarios.q: What is the core control?
opts: Check the link, eligibility and supporting evidence before reimbursement
scenarios.feedback: The claim should reconcile to the authorised mission and be supported by eligible, traceable evidence.

scenarios.title: Mission file is approved but evidence is stored separately
scenarios.q: What improves audit readiness?
opts: Keep approvals and expense evidence linked in one traceable file trail
scenarios.feedback: Audit readiness improves when authorisation, execution evidence, claim, approvals and reimbursement can be followed as one connected trail.

scenarios.title: Procurement file is complete except the approval evidence
scenarios.q: Is the audit trail complete?
opts: No, approval evidence is part of the decision trail
scenarios.feedback: A complete file shows not only the final contract but also who checked/approved the route and when.

scenarios.title: Final record location
scenarios.q: Where should the final record live?
opts: In the controlled DMS/project-file location with a traceable structure
scenarios.feedback: The final record should be maintained in the controlled project/DMS location so the evidence trail remains accessible and auditable.

scenarios.title: Decision trail
scenarios.q: What evidence should explain why a route was chosen?
scenarios.feedback: The file should preserve the reasoning for the route or decision, together with the resulting approvals and execution evidence.

scenarios.title: Tender file has evaluation scores but no conflict-of-interest declarations
scenarios.q: What is missing?
opts: A key integrity/control part of the evaluation trail
scenarios.feedback: Evaluation files should preserve the integrity trail, including the relevant declarations, authorisations and assessment record.

scenarios.title: Contract was amended but only the original contract is filed
scenarios.q: What should be added?
opts: The amendment, its justification/approval and related correspondence
scenarios.feedback: The file should show the complete contractual history, including amendments, supporting reasoning, approvals and execution evidence.

scenarios.title: Audit asks how an amount moved from decision to payment
scenarios.q: What should the file make possible?
opts: A traceable chain from decision → approval → contract/PO → delivery → invoice → payment
scenarios.feedback: An audit-ready file lets a reviewer follow the full evidence chain without reconstructing it from disconnected sources.

procurement.q: A staff member involved in a procedure may accept a small gift from a bidder, provided its value is modest.
procurement.explain: The value of gifts you may accept is zero: under the Council of Europe's no-gift policy, staff involved in procedures cannot receive any gifts or hospitality, regardless of value.
procurement.hint: Think about the exact gift value the guide allows.

procurement.q: From what estimated value (excl. VAT) must an international public call for tenders be used?
procurement.explain: From €184,000 the international public call for tenders applies and the Tenders Board is competent.
procurement.hint: It is also the Tenders Board threshold.

procurement.q: Paying an NGO to run its own project that also promotes Council of Europe values is a grant, not procurement.
procurement.explain: Procurement means buying for the Organisation's own needs. Covering the costs of a third party's own objectives is a grant under Rule No. 1374.
procurement.hint: Whose needs and objectives are being served?

procurement.q: What is the direct award ceiling for intellectual services?
procurement.explain: Low-value direct award is allowed up to €2,000 for goods, general services and works, and €6,000 for intellectual services, on a memorandum validated by the CCM (Art. 22.4).
procurement.hint: Intellectual services have a higher ceiling than goods.

procurement.q: In a competitive bidding procedure, how many suppliers must at least be invited?
procurement.explain: At least three suppliers must be invited (nine for a multiple framework contract with a pool of three). The CCM is responsible for the procedure.
procurement.hint: The same number as the minimum suppliers per framework agreement lot.

procurement.q: A competitive bidding purchase below €10,000 excl. VAT may compare the public prices of three or more suppliers instead of inviting tenders.
procurement.explain: Article 21.2 of Rule No. 1395 allows a public prices comparison below €10,000; screenshots of the prices compared must be archived.
procurement.hint: Look for the public prices purchase ceiling.

procurement.q: What is the maximum duration of a framework contract or framework agreement?
procurement.explain: Framework contracts and agreements should not exceed four years, or five exceptionally, to respect non-exclusivity and periodic competition.
procurement.hint: Periodic competition limits how long one supplier can be locked in.

procurement.q: How long must contractual and procurement documents be retained?
procurement.explain: All procurement documents must be archived for 10 years to support audits.
procurement.hint: Evaluate, learn, archive...

procurement.q: A project needs a trainer repeatedly in defined formats (one hour, half day, full day), but the total volume is unknown. Which contract type fits?
options: Framework contract with a price list per unit
procurement.explain: Recurring, unit-based needs that cannot be fully quantified suit a framework contract with fixed unit prices; the CCM signs each order after the PO is raised.
procurement.hint: The units can be defined, only the quantity is unknown.

procurement.q: An extrabudgetary-funded competitive bidding procedure of €90,000 can be submitted directly to the CCM for approval.
procurement.explain: Since 1 February 2025, extrabudgetary procedures between €55,000 and €184,000 need a DLAPIL Legal Compliance Review before the CCM approves the launch.
procurement.hint: Check the funding source and the €55,000 mark.

procurement.q: What must exist before the Organisation signs any contract?
procurement.explain: A PO is mandatory before signature, and no goods or services may be provided before the CCM countersigns: PO first, signature second, work third.
procurement.hint: The budget must be committed first.

procurement.q: What should the evaluation committee do with this bid?
procurement.scenario: In a €70,000 competitive bidding procedure, one bidder's offer arrives without one expert's CV and with the financial offer left blank. The other bids are complete.
options: Ask the bidder to send the CV and the financial offer
Ask only for the missing CV and score the bid
Exclude the bid, since a missing financial offer cannot be completed after opening
Score the technical part and estimate the price
procurement.explain: Under Art. 17.2 offers can be clarified but never changed. A missing CV may be clarified, but a missing financial offer would change the bid, so it is excluded.
procurement.hint: Clarifying versus changing an offer.

procurement.q: Which approach is correct?
procurement.scenario: A project expects 12 expert reports over its three-year life, each worth about €18,000. The manager proposes buying them one by one through separate competitive bidding procedures.
options: Run one competitive bidding procedure for the first year only
Estimate all 12 reports over the whole project (≈€216,000) and launch an international public call
Use direct award for each report as intellectual services
procurement.explain: The threshold is the total foreseeable value of the need over the whole project, including extensions; splitting it to avoid the €184,000 route is forbidden and the Tenders Board is competent.
procurement.hint: Calculate per need, not per order or year.

procurement.q: What is the safest procedure choice?
procurement.scenario: A team estimates €170,000 of translation services over four years under a voluntary contribution. The project is likely to be extended for a further year.
options: Competitive bidding now, and ask the Tenders Board later if needed
International public call for tenders from the start
Competitive bidding with an LCR, then amend the contract
procurement.explain: With a likely extension, the value may exceed €184,000; the Tenders Board cannot approve a launch retroactively, so an international call is needed from the outset.
procurement.hint: Include possible extensions in the estimate.

procurement.q: What should the buyer entity do now?
procurement.scenario: A framework contract awarded through competitive bidding has reached €150,000 in orders. More training sessions worth about €50,000 are planned for next year.
options: Ask the CCM to authorise a 10% increase
Keep ordering, as the ceiling applies per year
Contact DLAPIL and prepare an international call approved by the Tenders Board before spending exceeds €184,000
Sign an amendment raising the contract ceiling
procurement.explain: A framework contract awarded by competitive bidding cannot exceed €184,000 in total; amendments may never change its volume, so a new international call is required.
procurement.hint: The ceiling applies to cumulative spending.

procurement.q: If urgent needs arise because a team planned late, it may justify an exceptional direct award on grounds of urgency.
procurement.explain: Urgency justifies direct award only when it is unforeseen and not attributable to the buyer entity; the CCM (or the Tenders Board from €184,000) decides.
procurement.hint: Whose fault is the urgency?

procurement.q: Put the steps for an extrabudgetary-funded €120,000 competitive bidding procedure in the correct order.
options: Launch: invite at least three suppliers, preferably via e-procurement
Send a Request for LCR to DLAPIL
Prepare the tender file and act of engagement from fresh DLAPIL templates
DLAPIL issues its visa (within about 5 working days)
procurement.explain: Between €55,000 and €184,000 on extrabudgetary funds, the LCR comes before CCM approval, and no procedure is launched without approval.
procurement.hint: No approval, no launch; legal check before the CCM.

procurement.q: Order the closing steps of an international public call for tenders.
options: Sign the contract with the winner after the PO is raised
Assessors score bids and the buyer entity submits a reasoned recommendation
procurement.explain: The Tenders Board awards international calls on the buyer entity's reasoned recommendation; you sign with the winner first, then notify the others within 15 days.
procurement.hint: Sign with the winner first, then notify the others.

procurement.q: What is the correct next step?
procurement.scenario: An international call for €300,000 of event services, funded by the EU, produced three eligible offers, all well above the budget. The project still needs the services within six months.
options: Negotiate prices directly with the cheapest bidder
Award to the cheapest bidder and reduce the scope in the contract
Send a memo to the Tenders Board explaining the failure and asking to negotiate, relaunch or cancel
Switch to a competitive bidding procedure under the CCM
procurement.explain: Negotiation needs prior authorisation: for an international call the Tenders Board decides, on a memo justifying why the call failed and the option chosen.
procurement.hint: Seek authorisation before negotiating.

procurement.q: How should the buyer entity respond?
procurement.scenario: Two days before the deadline of a €200,000 call, a bidder asks whether a lower minimum turnover would be accepted. Another bidder asks privately what an unclear specification means.
options: Lower the turnover requirement for everyone and answer the second bidder privately
Refuse to change the criteria, and publish clarifications to all bidders no later than 48 hours before the deadline
Extend the deadline after it expires to allow new criteria
Answer each bidder individually by phone
procurement.explain: Published criteria can never be changed; clarifications are allowed but must be given to all bidders equally, with the last answer at least 48 hours before the deadline.
procurement.hint: Same answers to everyone; criteria are fixed once published.

grants.q: A grant must both help the grantee attain its own objectives and advance the Council of Europe's values or policies.
grants.explain: Under Rule 1374 the two purposes are cumulative: support for the grantee's goals and advancement of the Organisation's values or policies.
grants.hint: Are the two purposes alternatives or both required?

grants.q: Which instrument does Rule 1374 implement?
options: Article 43 bis of the Financial Regulations
The Statute of the Council of Europe, Article 1
grants.explain: Grants are provided for by Article 43 bis of the Financial Regulations, which Rule 1374 implements.
grants.hint: Think of the Financial Regulations.

grants.q: Rule 1374 applies only to grants financed from the Ordinary Budget.
grants.explain: Rule 1374 applies to all grant procedures whatever the source of funding: Ordinary Budget, Voluntary Contributions and agreements with external donors.
grants.hint: Consider voluntary contributions and EU funds.

grants.q: From what total estimated budget does a grant award procedure in principle require a call for proposals?
grants.explain: Procedures of € 15,000 or more require, in principle, a competitive call for proposals (Rule 1374, Art. 2.1); below that a direct award with Template G9.2A is possible.
grants.hint: The same figure separates G9.2A from the competitive route.

grants.q: Which principle requires the grantee to finance part of the action from its own or third-party resources?
grants.explain: The co-financing principle (Art. 2.3) means the Council does not fund the whole cost; it also distinguishes grants from service contracts.
grants.hint: It expresses the grantee's ownership of the action.

grants.q: Under the non-cumulative awards principle, the Council may award two different grants to the same project if each finances a different part of it.
grants.explain: Art. 2.4 allows only one Council grant per project or action, even where the financed parts are complementary.
grants.hint: Count the Council grants, not the cost lines.

grants.q: Who reviews a complaint first, to check for a manifest error?
grants.explain: Under Art. 15.4 the Co-ordinator makes an immediate preliminary examination for manifest error before any referral to the Review Board.
grants.hint: The person best able to grasp the file quickly.

grants.q: Who sits on the Review Board?
options: Representatives of the internal Auditor, the Director of Legal Advice (DLAPIL) and the Treasurer
grants.explain: Art. 15.6: the Review Board comprises representatives of the internal Auditor, DLAPIL and the Treasurer, none involved in the contested evaluation.
grants.hint: Independence from the evaluation is key.

grants.q: What is the maximum share of indirect eligible costs in a grant?
options: No ceiling if stated in the call
grants.explain: Art. 6.3 caps indirect costs at 7% of the total; the percentage must be stated in the call and made contractual in the agreement.
grants.hint: A single-digit ceiling.

grants.q: Which of the following is an ineligible cost?
options: Staff costs directly needed for the project
Debts incurred before the grant was awarded
Travel within the implementation period, shown in the budget
Indirect costs at 5% stated in the agreement
grants.explain: Art. 7.1 lists debts and provisions for losses incurred before the award as ineligible, applying Art. 6.2 a) and non-retroactivity.
grants.hint: Look for the cost that predates the award.

grants.q: Which template is used for a call for proposals funded by EU funds?
grants.explain: G8.1A is for the Ordinary Budget or Voluntary Contributions; G8.1B is the call template for EU funds (Art. 8).
grants.hint: B variants usually concern EU funds.

grants.q: A grant financed by the EU is awarded. Which agreement template do you use?
grants.explain: G17.2B is the grant agreement for EU funds; G17.2A is the grant agreement for the Ordinary Budget (BO) or Voluntary Contributions (VC). G8.1B is the call template and G9.2A the direct-award template.
grants.hint: Agreement templates are numbered G17; B variants concern EU funds.

grants.q: Which procedure applies?
grants.scenario: A department plans to award four grants of € 6,000 each to local NGOs for a youth campaign. The officer proposes four direct awards with Template G9.2A because each grant is under € 15,000.
options: A call for proposals is required in principle: the € 24,000 total budget is what counts
grants.explain: The € 15,000 threshold refers to the total estimated budget of the procedure, not the amount per grantee (Art. 2.1), so a call (G8.1A) is required in principle.
grants.hint: Which figure is compared with the threshold?

grants.q: Can these costs be accepted?
grants.scenario: The call closed on 1 March and the agreement is signed on 1 May. The grantee started work on 15 April and claims costs incurred from 15 February, before the closing date.
options: Yes, all costs since the project started
Only costs incurred after the closing date for submission; the February costs are ineligible
No: the project started before signature, so no grant can be signed
Yes, if the Commitments Officer approves in writing
grants.explain: Non-retroactivity (Art. 2.2.2) allows a project already begun at signature, but eligible costs cannot predate the closing date for proposals.
grants.hint: Separate the start of work from the date costs were incurred.

grants.q: What is the issue with this request?
grants.scenario: An association asks for an operational grant to cover its running costs from January of one year to June of the next, i.e. 18 consecutive months, in a single agreement.
options: None: operational grants have no duration limit
Operational grant agreements should not normally exceed twelve consecutive months
It must be turned into a service contract
It is allowed only if indirect costs exceed 7%
grants.explain: Rule 1374 states operational grants should not normally give rise to agreements longer than twelve consecutive months; G17.2A would cover a 12-month period.
grants.hint: Check the normal maximum duration for operational grants.

grants.q: Is this request for further information acceptable?
grants.scenario: During the eligibility check, the Co-ordinator asks an applicant to clarify a figure in its budget. The applicant replies with a revised budget adding a new activity and a higher co-financing rate, which would raise its score.
options: Yes, clarification requests may improve proposals
Only the clarification may be taken into account; the substantive changes must be disregarded
Yes, if all applicants are offered the same chance
The proposal must be excluded automatically
grants.explain: Requests for further information must not alter a proposal's content; substantive changes breach non-discrimination (Art. 11–12, report on G14.1).
grants.hint: Clarify versus modify.

grants.q: Put these steps of a competitive grant procedure (€ 15,000 or more) in the correct order.
options: Publication of the call for proposals (G8.1A/B)
grants.explain: The guide's summary: Co-ordinator (G3.1), call (G8.1A/B), questions, Evaluation Committee, opening (G11.1), assessment (G14.x), CCM decision (G14.6), then notification.
grants.hint: Someone must run the procedure before anything is published.

grants.q: Put the steps of the enquiry and complaint route of an unsuccessful applicant in order.
options: Complaint lodged within 30 calendar days of the reply to the enquiry
Review Board examines the complaint and issues an opinion (G15.7)
Enquiry within the deadline stated in letter G14.9A/B (minimum 7 days)
Co-ordinator's preliminary check for manifest error
grants.explain: Art. 15: an enquiry must precede a complaint; the Co-ordinator checks for manifest error first, and only otherwise refers it to the Review Board (opinion G15.7).
grants.hint: No complaint without a prior enquiry.

grants.q: How should this amendment request be handled?
grants.scenario: Halfway through a € 40,000 project grant under G17.2A, the grantee asks by email to extend the deadline by two months and to raise the grant to € 48,000 to cover unexpected price rises.
options: Accept both through a G17.3 amendment
The extension may be agreed in writing (e.g. G17.3 or email); the increase in the total amount must be refused
Refuse both: grant agreements can never be amended
Accept the increase, as it is below 20%
grants.explain: Art. 17.3: amendments may cover management aspects such as deadlines, but the total amount must not be increased, to avoid distorting the original competition.
grants.hint: Management details versus the conditions of the award.

grants.q: What is the correct handling of this complaint?
grants.scenario: An unsuccessful applicant, after receiving the reply to its enquiry, complains that one published award criterion was worded unfairly. It does not challenge how its proposal was examined.
options: Refer it to the Review Board for a fresh evaluation
Declare it inadmissible (G15.3A): only the way the proposal was examined can be contested
Ask the Evaluation Committee to reweight the criterion
Forward it to the internal Auditor as an allegation of misconduct
grants.explain: Under Art. 15.3 a complaint against the wording of published criteria, rather than their application, is inadmissible (Template G15.3A); published criteria cannot be altered.
grants.hint: What may a complaint actually contest?

Foundations: Confirm procurement—not a grant—is the correct instrument.
Confirm no known conflict of interest.
Apply equal treatment and transparency from the start.
Contract Types: Need pattern is classified: one-off / recurrent defined units / variable uncertain.
Contract type is not being confused with procedure type.
Framework duration and ordering method are defined where relevant.
No overlap with an existing framework contract/agreement.
Need & Planning: Similar foreseeable needs have been consolidated.
Existing contracts/database checked before launching a new tender.
Market analysis and supplier sourcing are proportionate to the need.
Reverse schedule includes approvals, publication, VAT and delivery.
Thresholds & Procedure: Total intended duration and renewals included.
Value assessed over the correct period of reference.
No artificial splitting or per-supplier calculation.
Funding source identified for validation route.
Tender Design: Exclusion, eligibility and award criteria defined before publication.
Eligibility criteria are measurable and proportionate.
Award criteria and weights are clear.
Submission, contractual and delivery conditions are complete.
Launch & Publication: At least three suppliers invited where competitive bidding is not published, or exception recorded.
Publication channel and deadline are documented.
E-procurement requirement checked for the current date/value.
Evaluation: At least two authorised staff analyse the tender as required by the guide.
Award scoring uses only published criteria with written reasons.
Clarification & Negotiation: All exchanges are written and retained.
Negotiation approval obtained from CCM/TB where required.
Negotiations do not significantly change tender specifications.
Final changes are confirmed by bidders in writing.
Award: Recommendation traces back to evaluation evidence.
Contract is concluded before unsuccessful bidders are notified.
Unsuccessful bidder notifications include reason and enquiry route.
Contract Signing: AoE/contract complete and signed by supplier.
PO/budgetary commitment created before Council signature.
No performance starts before Council signature.
Final signed documents sent and archived.
Contract Management: Delivery deadline and contract end date tracked separately.
Framework expenditure monitored against original threshold.
Supplier performance documented during and at end of contract.
Breach/termination steps documented and escalated where needed.
Contract Execution & Payment: VAT status and place of taxation clarified before signature.
Bank account matches contractual payment details.
Payment terms and any schedule reflected in contract.
Payment evidence is filed through the correct route.
Filing & Audit Trail: Tender documents and all bids archived.
Execution evidence retained by buyer entity.
Performance learning captured for future procurement.

procurementBestPractice.Need & Planning: Check the shared contract database and market before launching a new procedure. Use long-term planning to reduce repeated procurement effort.
procurementBestPractice.Thresholds & Procedure: If the estimate is close to €184,000, use the international route rather than risk exceeding the threshold later.
procurementBestPractice.Tender Design: Download a fresh template at the start of each procurement process because templates are updated over time.
procurementBestPractice.Launch & Publication: Publish at a sensible time and give suppliers a deadline proportionate to the complexity of the tender.
procurementBestPractice.Evaluation: Write clear, exhaustive reasons for technical/quality scores; strong documentation makes later enquiries and audits easier.
procurementBestPractice.Contract Management: Use reminders and proactive supplier communication before deadlines rather than reacting after a missed delivery date.
procurementBestPractice.Filing & Audit Trail: Archive as the process runs, not at the end. This preserves a cleaner and more reliable audit trail.

Foundations: Confirm grant is the correct instrument.
Identify funding source and donor conditions.
Costs: Each cost is necessary and budgeted.

grantBestPractice.Principles: Define co-financing, implementation timing and non-cumulative funding logic before publication; these are harder to correct later.
grantBestPractice.Criteria: Test every criterion before publication: Is it objective, proportionate, relevant and verifiable? Can the supporting document actually prove it?
grantBestPractice.Call & Publication: Use the call-content checklist and obtain legal input before publication where the draft includes special conditions or sensitive submission arrangements.
grantBestPractice.Evaluation: Separate the gates clearly: exclusion → eligibility → award. Keep reasoning and evidence at each stage so the final decision is traceable.
grantBestPractice.Agreement: Set the implementation period, reporting and payment architecture precisely before signature; later amendments cannot be used to redesign the award.
grantBestPractice.Filing: Archive progressively throughout the procedure rather than reconstructing the file at close-out.

buyer.name: Buyer entity / project team
buyer.summary: The Council of Europe entity for which the purchase is made. It runs the process from forecasting the need to executing the contract.
does: Defines needs and estimates the threshold
Prepares tender documents and technical specifications
Invites or publishes and answers questions
Submits files to the CCM or Tenders Board
Receives and accepts deliverables and verifies invoices
Monitors contract execution and supplier performance

authorised.name: Authorised staff members
authorised.summary: Members of the buyer entity authorised in writing by the CO or CCM (Rule No. 1395, Article 3.2.d) to perform key procedure tasks.
authorised.when: From approval of the tender documents until the award.
does: Open offers or represent the buyer entity at opening
Assess offers, with at least two assessors
Conduct negotiations with tenderers when authorised
Report indications of fraud or collusion

ccm.name: Commitments Officer / Cost Centre Manager
ccm.summary: COs authorise expenditure and delegate to CCMs. The CCM is responsible for the cost centre's purchases and decides on competitive bidding procedures and direct awards below €184,000.
ccm.when: At every validation and signature point.
does: Validates the choice of procedure and the tender documents
Authorises launch, deadline extensions and negotiations
Decides awards for competitive bidding procedures
Approves direct awards below €184,000
Signs contracts, orders and call-offs
Decides consequences of missed deadlines and approves amendments

tb.name: Tenders Board
tb.summary: Ensures compliance with the rules for all contracts above €184,000 excluding VAT. It is chaired by the Director General of Administration, with the DLAPIL Director, the Treasurer and an MAE member.
tb.when: For international public calls, direct awards from €184,000, call-offs above €184,000 and complaints.
does: Authorises the launch and publication of international calls
Scrutinises bid analyses and decides on awards
Authorises negotiations, amendments and direct awards
Decides on unfruitful or discontinued international calls
Rules on complaints within 30 days

tbsec.name: Secretariat of the Tenders Board
tbsec.summary: Part of the DGA's Legal Support Division. It runs the Tenders Board's calendar, templates, SharePoint and consultations, and checks files before submission.
tbsec.when: Before and during Tenders Board procedures.
does: Reviews files before they go to the Board
Runs electronic consultations with at least 48 hours for members
Publishes international calls after approval
Opens bids at cdm@coe.int when e-procurement is not used
Archives Tenders Board decisions

dlapil.name: DLAPIL
dlapil.summary: The Directorate of Legal Advice and Public International Law handles all legal procurement questions and templates. It performs the Legal Compliance Review for extrabudgetary-funded procedures from €55,000 to €184,000.
dlapil.when: For any legal question, and mandatorily for Legal Compliance Reviews.
does: Provides tender file, act of engagement and order form templates
Carries out the Legal Compliance Review within 5 working days
Advises on legal conditions, amendments and breaches
Provides third-party purchase templates on request
Trains staff on procurement procedures

pu.name: Procurement Unit (DGA)
pu.summary: Manages all DGA purchases and advises every buyer entity on non-legal procurement issues and tools, including e-procurement. It responds within a 48-hour SLA.
pu.when: From market analysis to contract execution.
does: Supports market analysis, sourcing and calls for expressions of interest
Maintains the suppliers and contracts databases
Supports e-procurement and OJEU publication
Provides analysis tables and expenditure tracking tools
Monitors procurement KPIs and purchase mapping

tpa.name: Treasury, Payments and Accounting (TPA)
tpa.summary: Registers suppliers and bank details in FIMS, checks payment claims and pays suppliers.
tpa.when: At supplier registration and at payment.
does: Processes MSA 4002 supplier creation in FIMS
Checks payment claims and settles invoices
Approves specific payment conditions
Provides card numbers for exceptional card payments
Keeps invoices and payment requests

dpc.name: Directorate of Programme Co-ordination (DPC)
dpc.summary: Co-ordinates programming and resource mobilisation for extrabudgetary co-operation projects and ensures they comply with the project management methodology.
does: Advises on existing framework contracts in external offices
Addresses donor visibility and communication requirements
Gives guidance on hiring civil servants from Horizontal Facility beneficiaries
Ensures activities match the approved project budget

dio.name: Directorate of Internal Oversight (DIO)
dio.summary: Provides independent audit, evaluation and investigation, including compliance and performance audits of procurement.
dio.when: When audits take place or wrongdoing is suspected.
does: Audits procurement compliance and performance
Receives reports of fraud, corruption and wrongdoing
Investigates suspected proscribed practices
Reports on risks detected in declarations of interests

0.what: The Council applies a no-gift policy: staff involved in procurement or grants cannot receive any gifts or hospitality from current or prospective contractors, whatever their value.
0.why: Accepting even a small gift breaches the Code of Conduct and can lead to disciplinary sanctions and tainted procedures.

Rule No. 1395.what: Rule No. 1395 of 20 June 2019 complements the Financial Regulations and lays down the details of every procurement procedure, from tender file to contract signature.
Rule No. 1395.why: All Council of Europe purchases must follow one of its procedures; an annotated version on the Tenders Board page answers recurring questions.

31 January.what: Staff involved in procurement must submit a declaration of interests each year by the end of January, or within one month of any change or of taking up duties.
31 January.why: The declaration (Rule No. 1282) is checked in audits and protects you and the procedure from conflict-of-interest challenges.

€184,000.what: The Tenders Board ensures compliance with the competitive tendering rules for all contracts exceeding €184,000 excluding VAT.
€184,000.why: Above this amount the Board must authorise the procedure beforehand; it cannot approve an international call retroactively.

€55,000–€184,000.what: Since 1 February 2025, competitive bidding and direct award procedures funded wholly or partly by extrabudgetary funds between €55,000 and €184,000 excl. VAT need a DLAPIL Legal Compliance Review.
€55,000–€184,000.why: The CCM or Commitments Officer may only approve the launch once the review is completed, so plan for it in your timetable.

48 h.what: The Procurement Unit (procurement@coe.int) operates a 48-hour service level for providing an initial response to queries.
48 h.why: Contact them early: a first answer comes within two days, but complex advice may take longer than your deadlines allow.

3.what: In a competitive bidding procedure the buyer entity must invite at least three potential suppliers to submit an offer (Rule 1395, Article 21.2).
3.why: The three must be meaningful candidates able to deliver good bids; inviting suppliers just to reach the number defeats competition.

50,000+.what: FIMS already holds over 50,000 supplier entries, but the renewal rate of active suppliers is very low.
50,000+.why: Relying only on known suppliers limits competition; actively look for new bidders through market research and CEIs.

Art. 5.what: Under Article 5 of Rule 1395 a call for expressions of interest seeks interest from capable suppliers and is explicitly not a procurement procedure.
Art. 5.why: A CEI only builds a list of potential suppliers; a contract still requires a proper procurement procedure afterwards.

2 years.what: For Ordinary Budget purchases, needs should be assessed over the whole two-year budget cycle when defining the requirement and threshold.
2 years.why: Splitting similar needs across the cycle risks applying the wrong threshold and procedure.

Whole project.what: For co-operation projects, foreseeable similar needs must be assessed over the whole project duration, including possible project extensions.
Whole project.why: Ignoring extensions can push spending above the threshold of the procedure used, a serious breach of the rules.

3 weeks.what: Under an international public call for tenders, the submission deadline cannot be shorter than three weeks from publication.
3 weeks.why: Higher-threshold procedures also need several validations, so build this minimum publication time into your planning.

3.what: Framework agreements are always multiple, and a minimum of three suppliers per lot (or per agreement without lots) is recommended.
3.why: Fewer suppliers undermines the mini-competition that makes each call-off competitive.

4 years.what: Framework contracts and framework agreements should not last more than four years, or five years in exceptional circumstances.
4 years.why: The limit respects non-exclusivity and periodic competitive tendering; longer contracts need strong justification.

2–3 months.what: Order forms or call-offs placed near expiry should not run beyond the contract's end date by more than two to three months.
2–3 months.why: A new contract should be concluded as soon as possible; long run-ons circumvent competitive tendering.

€2,000 / €6,000.what: Direct award is possible below €2,000 excl. VAT for goods and general services, and below €6,000 excl. VAT for intellectual services chosen on expertise.
€2,000 / €6,000.why: Above these ceilings at least a competitive bidding procedure is needed, and total spending under the contract must stay below them.

€184,000.what: Contracts with estimated total expenditure above €184,000 excl. VAT require an international public call for tenders authorised by the Tenders Board.
€184,000.why: If the estimate is close to €184,000, launch an international call: the Board cannot approve one retroactively.

€10,000.what: Within competitive bidding, purchases under €10,000 excl. VAT may be made by comparing publicly available prices of at least three suppliers instead of inviting tenders.
€10,000.why: Prices must be publicly visible, not quotes, and screenshots of the three suppliers must be kept on file.

20 points.what: The weighting of the financial offer cannot in principle be lower than 20 points, unless a minimum score or exclusion level is set.
20 points.why: Under-weighting price undermines value for money and the defensibility of the award decision.

Out of 10.what: Each technical or quality award criterion should be scored out of 10, then weighted according to the need, with a written justification for each score.
Out of 10.why: Consistent scoring and justifications make the ranking transparent and defensible against enquiries and complaints.

15–35%.what: When limiting financial dependence, a bid representing between 15% and 35% of the supplier's annual turnover is considered satisfactory.
15–35%.why: This replaces excessive turnover requirements that would shut out newly created or small suppliers.

180 days.what: Offers are valid for 180 calendar days from the submission deadline; the period can be increased after consulting DLAPIL.
180 days.why: After expiry bidders are no longer bound and may refuse to sign unless all agree in writing to extend.

3 weeks.what: In an international public call for tenders, the deadline for submission of offers cannot be shorter than three weeks.
3 weeks.why: The deadline must also be proportionate to complexity; too short a period reduces competition and can invalidate the procedure.

3 months.what: For tacit renewal, a three-month notice to object is usually considered reasonable, and the notice period may never be shorter than one month.
3 months.why: Without proper notice the contract renews automatically each year until its final end date.

5 working days.what: Complete requests for a Legal Compliance Review are processed by DLAPIL within 5 working days.
5 working days.why: Incomplete requests cause delays or requests for more information, and the launch cannot be approved before the review is done.

48 h.what: Tenders Board electronic consultations give members at least 48 hours (two working days) to approve; and no answers to bidders' questions are given later than 48 hours before the submission deadline.
48 h.why: Plan both margins: Board approval cannot be rushed, and late questions cannot be answered, so publish early and answer promptly.

48 h|Tenders Board consultation period.what: Tenders Board electronic consultations give members at least 48 hours (two working days) to approve a request.
48 h|Tenders Board consultation period.why: Board approval cannot be rushed: build these two working days into your launch schedule.

48 h|before deadline: last Q&A answer.what: No answers to bidders' questions are given later than 48 hours before the submission deadline.
48 h|before deadline: last Q&A answer.why: Late questions stay unanswered, so publish early and answer promptly to keep all bidders equally informed.

2.what: Bids must be opened and analysed by at least two authorised staff members of the buyer entity.
2.why: The four-eyes principle protects the integrity of the procedure and is checked during audits.

10.what: The maximum score per technical or quality criterion is 10, each score then being weighted and justified in writing.
10.why: Scores outside the published scale or without justification make the evaluation open to challenge.

Art. 17.2.what: Article 17.2 of Rule 1395 allows offers to be clarified or supplemented, but this must not change their principal features or distort competition.
Art. 17.2.why: Letting a bidder improve its offer through clarifications breaches equal treatment and can void the award.

15 days.what: Unsuccessful bidders must be informed in writing no later than 15 days after the contract with the selected supplier has been signed.
15 days.why: Sign first, then notify promptly; late notification breaches the rule and delays the enquiry and complaint periods.

7 days.what: Unsuccessful bidders may submit a written enquiry within seven days of notification of the outcome, answered without undue delay.
7 days.why: Clear, prompt answers to enquiries reduce the risk of formal complaints.

30 days.what: A bidder who considers an error affected the outcome may complain in writing to the Tenders Board within 30 days; the Board replies within 30 days.
30 days.why: Well-documented evaluations are your defence; a rejected complaint after an international call may go to an ad hoc review board.

MSA 4002.what: For a new supplier, the supplier identity must be created in FIMS using form MSA 4002, processed by the Treasury, Payments and Accounting Department.
MSA 4002.why: Without the FIMS record no purchase order or payment can be made to the supplier.

CCM.what: When an act of engagement is used for a one-off contract, the relevant CCM signs it unless he or she expressly delegates the power to sign.
CCM.why: A one-off contract is both a legal and a financial commitment, so the signatory must be duly authorised.

PO.what: All purchases must be subject to a budgetary commitment (purchase order in FIMS) before any contract is signed by the Organisation.
PO.why: Signing without a PO is a breach of financial rules, and no goods or services may be provided before signature.

3.what: If a supplier fails more than three times to justify not submitting a tender for call-offs, the Council may terminate the framework agreement with that supplier.
3.why: Unresponsive suppliers weaken mini-competitions; keep records of refusals to justify any termination.

€184,000.what: Expenditure under a framework contract concluded after competitive bidding must not exceed €184,000, the threshold that defined the procedure.
€184,000.why: Exceeding it is a severe breach; an international call approved by the Tenders Board must then cover the remaining needs.

10%.what: Small call-off amendments not affecting substance and not increasing the original value by more than 10% may be concluded with CCM authorisation.
10%.why: Increases above 10% require DLAPIL advice, as they may amount to an unlawful new award.

60 days.what: By default the Council pays 60 days from receipt of the invoice or execution of the contract, whichever is later.
60 days.why: Different terms are negotiable but must be approved by TPA; French law forbids terms above 60 days net.

€5,000.what: When payment by card is unavoidable, a single purchase may not exceed €5,000, with total monthly card purchases capped at €30,000 Organisation-wide.
€5,000.why: Payments are normally by bank transfer; a PO is needed first and larger amounts should go by transfer.

DAP.what: For goods, the recommended Incoterm is DAP (Delivered at Place) with delivery to a Council of Europe address.
DAP.why: The Incoterm fixes who bears transport costs, risks and customs formalities; a wrong one can create unexpected costs.

10 years.what: All contractual documents listed in Chapter 4.10 must be kept for 10 years.
10 years.why: Auditors and donors may request the full file long after the contract ends; missing records can make expenditure ineligible.

1–10.what: Supplier performance is typically assessed by questionnaire with questions scored, for example, from 1 (very poor) to 10 (very good).
1–10.why: Documented performance supports penalties and improves future tender documents, though poor past performance alone does not bar a supplier.

3 years.what: An optional exclusion criterion allows excluding suppliers who, in the previous three years, failed contractual obligations leading to refused payment or termination.
3 years.why: Blocklists are prohibited, so this documented criterion is the only lawful way to exclude past poor performers.

2.what: A grant must both assist the grantee in attaining its own objectives and advance the Organisation's values or policies; the two purposes are cumulative.
2.why: If either purpose is missing the arrangement is not a grant and may need to be a procurement contract instead.

Art. 43 bis.what: Grants are foreseen by Article 43 bis of the Financial Regulations, implemented by Rule 1374, which applies whatever the source of funding.
Art. 43 bis.why: Ordinary Budget, voluntary contributions and external funds all follow the same Rule 1374 procedures.

12 months.what: Operational grants should not normally give rise to grant agreements lasting more than twelve consecutive months.
12 months.why: Longer operational grants need justification and risk being seen as structural funding rather than support.

3.what: Above €15,000, non-publication is only justified by an unforeseeable emergency, the grantee's unique characteristics, or a project predetermining the grantees, e.g. by a donor.
3.why: Exceptions are strictly interpreted; an unjustified direct award breaches transparency and can make funds ineligible.

€15,000.what: The €15,000 threshold refers to the total estimated budget of the grant award procedure; at €15,000 or more a call for proposals is in principle required.
€15,000.why: Using the per-grant amount instead of the total budget leads to unlawful direct awards.

5 × €10,000.what: Awarding five grants of €10,000 gives a reference figure of €50,000, so the €15,000 threshold is exceeded and a call is required.
5 × €10,000.why: Splitting a budget into small grants does not avoid publication; the total procedure budget counts.

< €15,000.what: Below €15,000 a grant may be directly awarded using decision Template G9.2A (Rule 1374, Art. 2.1.2), which also appoints the Co-ordinator.
< €15,000.why: Even a direct award needs a documented decision and a written grant agreement.

≥ €15,000.what: Procedures of €15,000 or more require a competitive call for proposals, with Co-ordinator, Evaluation Committee, opening, evaluation and award decision.
≥ €15,000.why: Skipping the call without a valid exception breaches the principle of transparency.

G9.2B.what: A direct award of €15,000 or more is exceptional and uses Template G9.2B, with the CCM's decision duly motivated (Art. 2.1.3).
G9.2B.why: Without a solid justification under one of the strict exceptions, the award can be challenged by auditors or donors.

a–k.what: Article 3.1 lists the Commitments Officer's responsibilities a to k, from deciding on direct award and approving the call to signing, suspending, terminating or recovering grants.
a–k.why: Knowing who decides each step avoids decisions taken by unauthorised staff.

G3.1.what: Template G3.1 is the Commitments Officer's decision appointing the Co-ordinator responsible for the smooth running of the grant procedure.
G3.1.why: The Co-ordinator must be formally appointed before the call is run.

G13.1.what: Template G13.1 is the decision appointing the Evaluation Committee, accompanied by members' declarations.
G13.1.why: An evaluation by a committee not formally appointed is procedurally flawed.

Art. 31 FR.what: The Commitments Officer's responsibilities may be delegated in writing to a cost centre manager under the conditions of Article 31 of the Financial Regulations.
Art. 31 FR.why: Oral or informal delegation is invalid, so decisions taken under it may be challenged.

3.what: Three categories of criteria apply in sequence: exclusion grounds, eligibility criteria, then award criteria for proposals that pass the first two.
3.why: Each category has a specific purpose; mixing them, e.g. scoring eligibility, distorts the evaluation.

Weighted.what: Each award criterion must be weighted, and the weighting must be clearly indicated in the call for proposals.
Weighted.why: Weighting gives applicants a transparent indication of each criterion's importance and must stay unchanged to the end.

Art. 5.4.what: Under Article 5.4, criteria and their weighting published in the call cannot be altered under any circumstances during the procedure.
Art. 5.4.why: Changing criteria after publication breaches equal treatment and invalidates the evaluation.

7%.what: Indirect eligible costs, if foreseen, must be stated in the call and the agreement and may never exceed 7% of the total (Article 6.3).
7%.why: Amounts above the ceiling are ineligible and must be recovered.

a–g.what: Direct eligible costs must meet conditions a to g, including being necessary, actually incurred in the period, verifiable, substantiated and in the estimated budget.
a–g.why: Costs failing any condition are ineligible and may have to be recovered from the grantee.

a–h.what: Costs a to h are always ineligible, such as expenditure financed by other sources, debts, interest, land and buildings, exchange losses and loans to third parties.
a–h.why: Accepting them breaks Rule 1374 and leads to recovery procedures or donor refusals.

a–j.what: Article 8.3 requires every call for proposals to contain elements a to j, from objectives and co-financing to criteria, number of grantees and agreement terms.
a–j.why: A call missing a mandatory element breaches transparency and can compromise the whole procedure.

G8.1A / G8.1B.what: Template G8.1A is the call for proposals for Ordinary Budget or voluntary contribution funds; G8.1B is for EU funds.
G8.1A / G8.1B.why: Using the wrong template can omit donor-specific requirements.

G8.3.what: Template G8.3 is the quality control checklist used to verify that a call contains all required elements.
G8.3.why: Running the checklist before publication catches omissions that cannot be fixed once the call is out.

2 people.what: The Co-ordinator opens proposals but never alone: a member of the Evaluation Committee must be present.
2 people.why: Opening alone or before the deadline breaches transparency and should lead to cancellation of the procedure.

G11.1.what: Template G11.1 is the report on the opening of proposals, recording information and the identification number of each proposal.
G11.1.why: The report is the evidence of a regular opening if the procedure is later questioned.

Force majeure.what: A proposal received late may only be considered if the applicant proves force majeure; the Committee advises the Commitments Officer on it.
Force majeure.why: Accepting unjustified late proposals breaches equal treatment between applicants.

≥ 1.what: The Rule requires at least one staff member on every Evaluation Committee, and a majority of staff members is recommended.
≥ 1.why: Staff members guard against conflicts of interest and ensure knowledge of the rules.

G13.4.what: Template G13.4 is the declaration of absence of conflicts of interests, signed by all Evaluation Committee members.
G13.4.why: An undeclared conflict can invalidate the evaluation and the award.

G13.5.what: Template G13.5 is the declaration of confidentiality, required only for Evaluation Committee members who are not Secretariat staff.
G13.5.why: External members are not bound by staff rules, so their written undertaking protects applicants' data.

0–5.what: Each Committee member individually scores every award criterion or sub-criterion out of 5, from 0 (fails or cannot be assessed) to 5 (excellent), with explanatory comments.
0–5.why: Consistent use of the scale and comments underpins the consensus report and defends against complaints.

15 days.what: The Commitments Officer must inform unsuccessful applicants in writing no later than 15 calendar days after the successful ones; this deadline is imperative.
15 days.why: Late notification breaches the Rule; best practice is to inform all applicants at the same time.

7 days.what: The letter to unsuccessful applicants must explain how to request information and give a cut-off date of at least 7 calendar days (Article 14.9).
7 days.why: Without this information, the enquiry and complaint deadlines cannot run properly.

G14.6.what: Template G14.6 is the Commitments Officer's decision on the award in a competitive procedure, based on the Committee's consensus report.
G14.6.why: The award must be a formal, documented decision by the competent officer before agreements are signed.

3.what: The Review Board comprises representatives of the internal Auditor, the Director of Legal Advice and Public International Law, and the Treasurer.
3.why: Members must not have been involved, even indirectly, in the evaluation challenged, to avoid bias.

30 days.what: Applicants may lodge a complaint within 30 calendar days of notification of the reply to their enquiry, and the Review Board meets within 30 calendar days of receiving it.
30 days.why: An enquiry must precede a complaint; missing either deadline affects admissibility or breaches the Rule.

30 days|calendar days to lodge a complai.what: Applicants may lodge a complaint within 30 calendar days of notification of the reply to their enquiry.
30 days|calendar days to lodge a complai.why: An enquiry must come first; a complaint lodged after 30 days is not admissible.

30 days|for the Review Board to meet aft.what: The Review Board meets within 30 calendar days of receiving a complaint.
30 days|for the Review Board to meet aft.why: Missing this deadline breaches the Rule, so convene the Board as soon as a complaint arrives.

Written.what: Signing a written grant agreement between the parties is imperative; any verbal agreement is contrary to the Rule.
Written.why: Without a written agreement there is no enforceable basis for payment, reporting or recovery.

G17.2A / G17.2B.what: Template G17.2A is the model grant agreement for Ordinary Budget or voluntary contribution funds; G17.2B is for EU funds.
G17.2A / G17.2B.why: The models contain mandatory clauses, such as data publication, that ad hoc drafts may omit.

G17.3.what: Template G17.3 is used to amend a grant agreement, which must always include a description of the action and an estimated budget.
G17.3.why: Changes not formalised by amendment are not binding and can make expenditure ineligible.

Initiating department.what: All documents from the Co-ordinator's appointment to validation of supporting documents must be kept by the department that initiated the grant procedure.
Initiating department.why: Auditors and donors expect one complete file; scattered records make it hard to justify the award.

Art. 19.what: Under Article 19, the Rule must be interpreted in good faith, in keeping with its spirit and the general principles in its Preamble.
Art. 19.why: Where the text is silent, choose the reading that best respects transparency and equal treatment.

[XX].what: Templates contain comments, blue highlighted parts and bracketed [XX] options that must all be completed or deleted before sending documents to third parties.
[XX].why: Sending templates with leftover options or comments looks unprofessional and can create contractual ambiguity.

financeConcepts.title: Financial Report
financeConcepts.definition: The controlled view of the project’s current financial position, built from actual expenditure, commitments and the available financial information.
financeConcepts.purpose: Establish a reliable baseline before any forward-looking planning or budget change is introduced.
financeConcepts.when: Use the latest reconciled Financial Report as the starting point for the Forecast & Budget Revision exercise.

financeConcepts.title: Forecast
financeConcepts.definition: The forward-looking financial picture that combines the current position with expected expenditure for the remaining implementation period.
financeConcepts.purpose: Estimate where the project is expected to finish financially and identify future funding pressures, savings or implementation needs.
financeConcepts.when: Prepare it after the current financial position is established and before the formal route is determined.

financeConcepts.title: Budget Revision
financeConcepts.definition: The controlled revision of the approved budget structure or figures when implementation no longer fits the current financial plan.
financeConcepts.purpose: Translate identified implementation changes into a revised budget that can be reviewed, justified and formally processed.
financeConcepts.when: Use it when the Forecast identifies reallocations, new budget lines, total-cost changes, an extension or changes in scope, purpose or objectives.
financeConcepts.output: Revised Budget + Variation / Budget Proposal package

financeConcepts.title: Formal Route
financeConcepts.definition: The formal action required once the revised budget and proposed changes have been reviewed.
financeConcepts.purpose: Determine the applicable approval, acceptance and documentation route for the revised project budget.
financeConcepts.when: For Joint Programmes, route logic leads to Notification or Addendum; for Voluntary Contributions, the applicable donor-acceptance route is used.

financeLifecycle.title: Financial Reporting
financeLifecycle.question: Where are we now?
financeLifecycle.lead: Establish the current financial position before making any forward-looking decision.
financeLifecycle.learn: Actual expenditure, commitments and the current reporting position.

financeLifecycle.title: Forecast
financeLifecycle.question: Where will we be at project end?
financeLifecycle.lead: Build the expected financial position using actual, committed and planned expenditure.
financeLifecycle.learn: Staff, office and activity expenditure through the remaining implementation period.

financeLifecycle.title: Variance & Review
financeLifecycle.question: Does the current budget still work?
financeLifecycle.lead: Compare the forecast with the approved/current budget before deciding whether a change is necessary.
financeLifecycle.learn: Savings, pressure points, overspend risk and movements between Budget Headings.

financeLifecycle.title: Change Assessment
financeLifecycle.question: What needs to change?
financeLifecycle.lead: Identify all changes together rather than treating each one as an isolated process.
financeLifecycle.learn: Reallocation, new budget line, total-cost change, extension and scope/objective change.

financeLifecycle.title: Decision
financeLifecycle.question: Does it require formal action?
financeLifecycle.lead: Determine the applicable formal route only after the revised financial picture is clear.
financeLifecycle.learn: JP route logic and the separate VC funding/acceptance route.
financeLifecycle.output: No action / Notification / Addendum / VC route

financeLifecycle.title: Prepare & Submit
financeLifecycle.question: What do I need to prepare?
financeLifecycle.lead: Turn the confirmed route into a complete donor-facing package and send it through the correct validation chain.
financeLifecycle.learn: Revised Budget, Variation, justification, Budget Proposal, validation and submission.

financeLifecycle.title: Update & Follow-up
financeLifecycle.question: What happens afterwards?
financeLifecycle.lead: Close the change by updating the project baseline and records used for the next reporting cycle.
financeLifecycle.learn: PMM, Delegation Letter, Fiche Staff and retained approval evidence.

po-file.title: Prepare a PO file
po-file.lead: Build a complete, signature-ready and audit-ready purchase order file for the selected service type.
po-file.remember: No activity starts before the PO is issued and documents are countersigned.
po-file.understand: The PO is the commitment that allows work to start, so it must rest on confirmed budget, a valid supplier route and the correct signatures.
po-file.do: Confirm the budget, the PMM activity ID and the supplier in FIMS, prepare the contractual package, obtain prior CCM approval and submit the complete file so that the ACCM can create the PO.
po-file.check: The PO has been issued, the contract was signed and dated after the PO and before delivery, the countersigned documents have been returned to the supplier and the issued PO is kept in the file.
figures: Submit the PO request at least two weeks before the scheduled start date to leave enough time for approval.

Procurements in the €55,000 to €184,000 band should follow the applicable legal and procurement review route.
